p.src: Now Fa Zheng met the man, and the two clapped their hands and laughed. Pang Tong asked who he was, and Fa Zheng replied, “This gentleman is from Guanghan. His surname is Peng, his given name is Yang, and his courtesy name is Yongyan. He is a man of outstanding talent in Shu. For speaking frankly and offending Liu Zhang, he was put in the cangue and reduced to penal servitude; that is why his hair is short.” Pang Tong received him with the courtesy due a guest and asked where he had come from. Peng Yang said, “I have come expressly to save the lives of your tens of thousands of men. I can speak only after I have seen General Liu.” Fa Zheng hurried to report this to Xuande. Xuande came to meet him in person and asked the reason for his visit. Peng Yang asked, “How many troops and horses does the general have in the forward camp?” Xuande answered truthfully, “Huang Zhong and Wei Yan are stationed there.” Peng Yang said, “How can one serve as a commander without understanding the terrain? The forward camp stands beside the Fu River. If the river is breached and troops block both front and rear, not one man will escape.” Xuande suddenly understood. Peng Yang said, “The Dipper Star lies in the west, and Venus has come over this place. Some misfortune is bound to occur, so you must be exceedingly cautious.” Xuande at once appointed Peng Yang to his staff, then secretly sent word to Wei Yan and Huang Zhong, ordering them to patrol vigilantly by day and night against any attempt to release the waters. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan conferred: “Each of us will take watch on alternate days; if enemy troops appear, we shall immediately inform each other.”

p.src: Now Leng Bao saw that wind and rain had risen fiercely that night. Leading five thousand troops straight along the riverbank, he prepared to breach the river, when suddenly a great clamor arose behind him. Realizing that preparations had been made against him, Leng Bao hastily turned his army back. Wei Yan came in pursuit with his troops, and the soldiers of Shu trampled one another. As Leng Bao fled, he ran straight into Wei Yan. After only a few exchanges on horseback, Wei Yan captured him alive. By the time Wu Lan and Lei Tong came to his aid, Huang Zhong’s force had also charged upon them. Wei Yan escorted Leng Bao to Fu Pass. Xuande rebuked him: “I treated you with benevolence and honor and released you to return home. How dare you betray me! This time you shall not be spared!” He had Leng Bao taken out and beheaded, and rewarded Wei Yan handsomely. Xuande gave a banquet in Peng Yang’s honor. Suddenly it was reported that Zhuge Liang, the military adviser in Jingzhou, had specially sent Ma Liang with a letter. Xuande summoned him and questioned him. When Ma Liang had completed his courtesies, he said, “All is peaceful in Jingzhou; my lord need not be concerned.” He then presented the military adviser’s letter. Xuande opened and read it. In essence it said: “Last night I calculated by the Taiyi method. This year is Guihai, and the Dipper Star lies in the west; I have also observed the celestial signs and seen Venus over the sector of Luo City, signifying much ill fortune and little good for the commanding general. You must be exceedingly cautious.”

p.src: After reading the letter, Xuande told Ma Liang to return ahead of him. Xuande said, “I shall return to Jingzhou and discuss this matter.” Pang Tong thought privately, “Kongming fears that I will conquer the western province and win the glory, so he has deliberately sent this letter to hinder me.” He therefore said to Xuande, “I too have calculated by the Taiyi method and already knew that the Dipper Star was in the west. It signifies that my lord is destined to gain Western River; it foretells no other calamity. I also observed the heavens and saw Venus over Luo City. Since the Shu general Leng Bao has already been beheaded, the evil omen has been fulfilled. My lord must not harbor doubts. We should advance without delay.”

p.src: Seeing Pang Tong urge him repeatedly, Xuande at last led the army forward. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan met him and escorted him into the camp. Pang Tong asked Fa Zheng, “How many routes lead onward to Luo City?” Fa Zheng drew a map upon the ground. Xuande took out the map Zhang Song had left him and compared the two; there was no discrepancy. Fa Zheng said, “North of the mountain lies a broad road leading directly to the east gate of Luo City; south of the mountain lies a narrow road leading to the west gate of Luo City. The army may advance by either route.” Pang Tong said to Xuande, “I shall appoint Wei Yan as vanguard and advance by the southern narrow road; my lord should appoint Huang Zhong as vanguard and advance by the broad road north of the mountain. We shall rendezvous at Luo City.” Xuande said, “From childhood I have been well practiced in archery and horsemanship, and I have often traveled narrow paths. The military adviser may take the broad road to the east gate; I shall take the west gate.” Pang Tong said, “Enemy troops are certain to intercept us on the broad road. My lord should lead his men against them. I shall take the narrow road.” Xuande said, “You must not, Adviser. Last night I dreamed that a divine figure struck my right arm with an iron staff, and even after waking my arm still ached. Perhaps this expedition will end badly.” Pang Tong said, “When brave warriors enter battle, it is only natural that they should die or suffer wounds. Why should a mere dream make you suspicious?” Xuande said, “What troubles me is Kongming’s letter. What if you remained to guard Fu Pass?” Pang Tong laughed loudly and said, “My lord has been misled by Kongming. He does not wish me alone to accomplish this great feat, so he said these things to sow doubt in my lord’s mind. Doubt in the mind gives rise to dreams; what ill omen can there be? Only if I spill my brains upon the ground will I prove true to my deepest resolve. My lord, say no more. We shall set out tomorrow morning without fail.” Orders were issued that very day for the soldiers to cook at the fifth watch and mount at daybreak. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan led their forces out first. As Xuande was once more settling the plan with Pang Tong, Pang Tong’s mount suddenly shied at something unfamiliar before it and threw him to the ground. Xuande leapt from his horse and personally caught hold of the animal. Xuande said, “Why does the military adviser ride such a wretched horse?” Pang Tong replied, “I have ridden this horse a long time, and it has never behaved like this before.” Xuande said, “If it shies in battle, it may cost a man his life. The white horse I ride is exceedingly tame and reliable. The military adviser may ride it, and then nothing can possibly go wrong. I shall ride the inferior horse myself.” He then exchanged mounts with Pang Tong. Pang Tong thanked him, saying, “I am profoundly grateful for my lord’s generous kindness. Even if I died ten thousand deaths, I could never repay it.” They each mounted and set off along their respective routes. As Xuande watched Pang Tong depart, he felt deeply uneasy and went on his way in dejection.

p.src: Meanwhile, in Luo City, Wu Yi and Liu Gui learned that Leng Bao had been lost and conferred with the others. Zhang Ren said, “There is a narrow road in a secluded part of the mountains southeast of the city. It is of the utmost importance, so I shall personally lead a force to guard it. You gentlemen must defend Luo City closely and allow no mishap.” Suddenly came a report that the Han army was approaching in two columns to attack the city. Zhang Ren hurriedly led three thousand troops ahead to lay an ambush along the narrow road. When he saw Wei Yan’s troops pass, Zhang Ren ordered his men to let them all through without raising the alarm. Later, when Pang Tong’s army approached, Zhang Ren’s soldiers pointed from afar at the general in its midst and said, “The man riding the white horse must be Liu Bei.” Zhang Ren was overjoyed and issued orders for his men to act according to his plan.

p.src: Meanwhile, Pang Tong proceeded slowly onward. Looking up, he saw two mountains closing in narrowly, thick with tangled trees; and as it was the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, the branches and leaves grew luxuriantly. Pang Tong grew deeply suspicious. Reining in his horse, he asked, “What is the name of this place?” Among his men was a newly surrendered soldier, who pointed and said, “This place is called Fallen Phoenix Slope.” Pang Tong exclaimed in alarm, “My sobriquet is Young Phoenix, and this place is called Fallen Phoenix Slope. It bodes ill for me.” He ordered the rear ranks to retreat at once. Just then a cannon sounded from the slope ahead, and arrows flew like locusts, all aimed at the rider on the white horse. p.src: That day, after Zhang Ren had shot Pang Tong dead, the Han troops became jammed together, unable either to advance or retreat, and more than half were killed. The vanguard hastened to report the disaster to Wei Yan. Wei Yan hurriedly reined in his troops and tried to turn back, but the mountain road was so narrow that they could not fight effectively. Zhang Ren had also cut off his route of retreat and was shooting down from high ground with powerful bows and heavy crossbows, throwing Wei Yan into alarm. One of the newly surrendered Shu soldiers said, “We would do better to fight our way to the foot of Luo City and then advance by the broad road.”

p.src: Wei Yan followed his advice, took the lead in clearing a path, and fought his way toward Luocheng. Where the dust rose, an army charged in from ahead, led by Wu Lan and Lei Tong, the defenders of Luocheng; while Zhang Ren led troops in pursuit from behind. Attacked from front and rear, Wei Yan was surrounded in the heart of the battlefield. Wei Yan fought desperately but could not break free. Suddenly, the rear ranks of Wu Lan and Lei Tong fell into disorder, and the two commanders hastily wheeled their horses around to rescue them. Wei Yan seized the moment and pursued them. At the head of the oncoming force, a commander brandished his blade, spurred his horse forward, and shouted, “Wenchang, I have come especially to save you!” Wei Yan looked and saw that it was the veteran general Huang Zhong. Attacking from both sides, they defeated Wu Lan and Lei Tong and drove straight to the foot of Luocheng’s walls. Liu Gui led troops out to attack, but Xuande blocked him from the rear and provided support. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan turned about and withdrew.

p.src: Just as Xuande’s army was hurrying back to camp, Zhang Ren’s troops emerged from a narrow road and cut them off. Liu Gui, Wu Lan, and Lei Tong came foremost in pursuit. Unable to hold either camp, Xuande fought as he retreated and fled back to Fu Pass. Victorious, the Shu troops pursued them without respite. Xuande’s men were exhausted and their horses spent; they had no heart for battle and thought only of escape. As they neared Fu Pass, Zhang Ren’s army pressed the pursuit ever harder. Fortunately, Liu Feng on the left and Guan Ping on the right led thirty thousand fresh troops out to intercept the enemy and drove Zhang Ren back; they pursued him for another twenty li and recaptured a great many warhorses.

p.src: Xuande and his whole force reentered Fu Pass. He asked for news of Pang Tong. A soldier who had escaped alive from Fallen Phoenix Slope reported, “The military adviser and his horse were both shot dead before the slope in a storm of arrows.” On hearing this, Xuande faced west and wept without cease, then summoned Pang Tong’s spirit from afar and offered sacrifices to him. All the commanders wept as well. Huang Zhong said, “Now that we have lost Military Adviser Pang Tong, Zhang Ren will surely come to attack Fu Pass. What are we to do? We had better send someone to Jingzhou and ask Military Adviser Zhuge to come and deliberate on a plan to take Yi Province.” As he spoke, a messenger reported that Zhang Ren had led his army directly beneath the walls and was challenging them to battle. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan both vied to go out and fight. Xuande said, “Our fighting spirit has just suffered a reverse. We should hold fast until the military adviser arrives.” Huang Zhong and Wei Yan obeyed and confined themselves to guarding the city closely. Xuande wrote a letter and instructed Guan Ping, “Go to Jingzhou for me and summon the military adviser.” Guan Ping took the letter and hurried to Jingzhou by night and day. Xuande himself guarded Fu Pass and did not go out to battle.

p.src: Meanwhile, Kongming was in Jingzhou. On the festival of the Seventh Night, he held a grand evening banquet for the officials, and they discussed the conquest of Yi Province. Suddenly, directly to the west, a star as large as a dipper fell from the sky, scattering streams of light in every direction. Kongming started in alarm, dashed his cup to the ground, covered his face, and cried, “Alas! What grief!” The officials anxiously asked him why. Kongming said, “I calculated earlier that this year the baleful star lay in the west, an ill omen for a military adviser; the Celestial Hound encroached upon our army, and the Great White Star stood over Luocheng. I had already written to our lord, urging him to guard carefully against disaster. Who would have thought that tonight a star would fall in the west? Pang Shiyuan’s life must surely be ended!” Having said this, he wept bitterly and cried, “My lord has now lost one of his arms!” All the officials were astonished, but did not yet believe his words. Kongming said, “News will surely arrive within a few days.” That evening, the banquet broke up without merriment.

p.src: Several days later, as Kongming sat with Yunchang and the others, a messenger announced Guan Ping’s arrival. All the officials were startled. Guan Ping entered and presented Xuande’s letter. Kongming read it. It said, “On the seventh day of the seventh month this year, Military Adviser Pang was shot and killed by Zhang Ren before Fallen Phoenix Slope.” Kongming wept bitterly, and not one of the officials could keep from shedding tears. Kongming said, “Since our lord is at Fu Pass, caught in a position where he can neither advance nor retreat, I, Liang, have no choice but to go.” Yunchang said, “If you leave, Military Adviser, who will defend Jingzhou? Jingzhou is a vital stronghold, and the responsibility is no small matter.” Kongming said, “Though our lord has not explicitly named the man in his letter, I already understand his intention.” He showed Xuande’s letter to the officials and said, “In this letter our lord entrusts Jingzhou to me and bids me judge whom best to appoint. Even so, by sending Guan Ping with the letter, he means for Lord Yunchang to assume this grave responsibility. Lord Yunchang, remember the bond sworn in the Peach Garden and exert all your strength to defend this land. The responsibility is weighty; you must do your utmost.” Yunchang declined no further and resolutely accepted the charge. Kongming gave a banquet and formally handed over the seals and insignia of office. Yunchang reached out with both hands to receive them. Holding up the seals, Kongming said, “The whole responsibility now rests upon you, General.” Yunchang said, “Once a true man accepts a grave duty, only death can bring him rest.” When Kongming heard Yunchang speak the word “death,” he was displeased at heart; he wanted to withhold the seals, but his word had already been given. Kongming asked, “What will you do if Cao Cao leads an army here?” Yunchang replied, “I shall resist him with all my strength.” Kongming asked again, “What if Cao Cao and Sun Quan both raise armies against you?” Yunchang replied, “I shall divide my forces and resist them both.” Kongming said, “If you do that, Jingzhou will be in peril. I have eight words for you. Remember them well, General, and you will be able to safeguard Jingzhou.” Yunchang asked what the eight words were. Kongming said, “Resist Cao Cao in the north; make peace with Sun Quan in the east.” Yunchang said, “I shall engrave the military adviser’s words upon my heart.”

Yunchang replied, “I shall resist him with all my strength.”
Kongming asked again, “What if Cao Cao and Sun Quan both raise armies against you?”
Yunchang replied, “I shall divide my forces and resist them both.”
Kongming said, “If you do that, Jingzhou will be in peril.
I have eight words for you. Remember them well, General, and you will be able to safeguard Jingzhou.”
Yunchang asked what the eight words were.
Kongming said, “Resist Cao Cao in the north; make peace with Sun Quan in the east.”
Yunchang said, “I shall engrave the military adviser’s words upon my heart.”

p.src: Kongming then gave him the seals and insignia, and ordered the civil officials Ma Liang, Yi Ji, Xiang Lang, and Mi Zhu, together with the military officers Mi Fang, Liao Hua, Guan Ping, and Zhou Cang, to assist Yunchang and join him in defending Jingzhou. Meanwhile, he himself would lead an army into Yi Province. First he detached ten thousand elite troops and placed them under Zhang Fei, ordering him to take the main road and fight his way toward Bazhou, west of Luocheng; whoever arrived first would claim the foremost merit. He detached another force, appointed Zhao Yun as its vanguard, and ordered it to sail upstream and rendezvous at Luocheng. Kongming followed afterward, setting out with Jian Yong, Jiang Wan, and the others. Jiang Wan, whose style name was Gongyan, was a native of Xiangxiang in Lingling; he was a noted scholar of the Jing-Xiang region and was then serving as a secretary.

p.src: That day, Kongming led fifteen thousand troops forth, setting out at the same time as Zhang Fei. As Zhang Fei was about to depart, Kongming admonished him, “Western Yi has many heroes; you must not underestimate the enemy. Along the way, strictly command the entire army not to plunder the people and thereby lose their goodwill. Wherever you go, show the people care and compassion, and do not wantonly have the soldiers flogged. I trust you will reach Luocheng early, General, without fail.”

p.src: Zhang Fei gladly accepted his orders, mounted his horse, and rode away, advancing steadily onward. Wherever the people submitted, he did not allow so much as a hair to be harmed. He proceeded directly along the Hanchuan road. When he reached Ba Commandery, a scout returned and reported, “Yan Yan, the governor of Ba Commandery, is a renowned general of Shu; though advanced in years, his vigor has not declined; he is skilled with a powerful bow and wields a great saber; his valor is such that he could withstand ten thousand men; he holds the city fast and has raised no flag of surrender.” Zhang Fei ordered camp to be pitched ten li from the city and sent a man inside with this message: “Tell that old wretch to come and surrender at once, and I shall spare the lives of everyone in the city! If he refuses submission, I shall raze the city and spare neither old nor young!”

p.src: Now Yan Yan was in Ba Commandery. When he heard that Liu Zhang had sent Fa Zheng to invite Xuande into Yi Province, he beat his breast and sighed, “This is what they call sitting alone on a barren mountain and inviting in a tiger for protection!” Later, hearing that Xuande had occupied Fu Pass, he was furious and repeatedly wished to lead his troops against him, but feared that enemy forces might come along this road. That day, learning that Zhang Fei’s army had arrived, he mustered the five or six thousand troops under his command and prepared to meet the enemy. Someone offered this counsel: “At Changban in Dangyang, a single roar from Zhang Fei drove back Cao Cao’s million-strong host. Even Cao Cao shuns him at the mere report of his approach; he must not be underestimated. For now, we should dig deep moats, raise high ramparts, and hold fast without going out. His army has no provisions; within a month at most, it will withdraw of its own accord. Moreover, Zhang Fei’s temper is like a raging fire, and he is forever flogging his soldiers. If we refuse him battle, he is sure to grow angry. And in his anger, he will surely treat his men with savage cruelty. Once their loyalty wavers, we can strike at the opportunity and capture Zhang Fei.” Yan Yan accepted this counsel and ordered every soldier to mount the walls and defend them. Suddenly a soldier appeared, shouting, “Open the gate!” Yan Yan ordered that he be admitted and questioned. The soldier said that General Zhang had sent him, and faithfully repeated Zhang Fei’s words. Yan Yan flew into a rage and cursed him: “How dare that wretch be so insolent! Would General Yan ever surrender to rebels? Take these words back to Zhang Fei!” He summoned his guards, had them cut off the soldier’s ears and nose, and then sent him back to camp.

p.src: The soldier returned to Zhang Fei and tearfully reported how Yan Yan had mutilated him and hurled insults. Zhang Fei was enraged. Grinding his teeth and glaring, he armed himself, mounted his horse, and led several hundred riders beneath the walls of Ba Commandery to challenge the enemy. The soldiers on the walls assailed him with every manner of abuse. Impatient by nature, Zhang Fei charged the drawbridge several times, trying to cross the moat, but each time a shower of arrows drove him back. By evening not a single man had come out, and Zhang Fei returned to camp with his belly full of rage. Early the next morning, he again led his army out to issue a challenge. From the gate tower, Yan Yan shot an arrow that struck Zhang Fei’s helmet. Pointing at him, Zhang Fei cried bitterly, “When I seize you, old wretch, I shall eat your flesh myself!” At evening he again returned empty-handed. On the third day, Zhang Fei led out his troops and marched around the city hurling abuse. The city was in fact a mountain stronghold, surrounded on every side by rugged peaks. Zhang Fei rode up a mountain and looked down into the city. He saw every soldier fully armed and drawn up in ranks, lying in wait within, but refusing to come out. He also saw laborers coming and going, carrying bricks and stones to help defend the city. Zhang Fei ordered his cavalry to dismount and his infantry to sit down, hoping to lure the enemy out, but there was no response. After another full day of abuse, he returned empty-handed as before. Back in camp, Zhang Fei thought, “I curse them all day, but they simply will not come out. What am I to do?” Suddenly a plan occurred to him. He ordered the main force to cease challenging the enemy, make every preparation, and wait in camp for battle. He sent only thirty or fifty soldiers straight beneath the walls to shout abuse, intending to fight if they could lure Yan Yan’s troops out. Zhang Fei rubbed his fists and palms, waiting only for the enemy to come. The soldiers cursed them for three days in succession, yet no one came out. Zhang Fei knitted his brows and devised another plan. He ordered his soldiers to scatter, cut firewood and fodder, and search for paths, without returning to challenge the city. Inside the city, Yan Yan grew suspicious after seeing no activity from Zhang Fei for several days. He had a dozen or so soldiers disguise themselves as Zhang Fei’s woodcutters, slip out of the city, mingle with his men, and enter the mountains to gather intelligence.

p.src: That day, all the troops returned to camp. Seated in camp, Zhang Fei stamped his feet and cursed, “That old wretch Yan Yan is driving me to death with rage!” Then three or four men before his tent said, “General, you need not distress yourself. Over the past few days, we have discovered a narrow path by which we can secretly pass around Ba Commandery.” Zhang Fei deliberately shouted, “If there is such a way, why did you not report it sooner?” They replied, “We have only just succeeded in scouting it out these past few days.” Zhang Fei said, “There is no time to lose. Cook the meal at the second watch tonight. At the third watch, while the moon is bright, we shall strike camp and depart. Let every man hold a gag in his mouth and remove the bells from the horses, and advance in silence. I shall open the way in front; the rest of you will follow in order.” Once the order had been issued, it was announced throughout the camp.

p.src: The soldiers spying on the enemy heard this news and all returned to the city to report it to Yan Yan. Yan Yan was delighted. “I knew that wretch would be unable to contain himself! If you steal through the narrow path, your provisions, fodder, and baggage must follow behind. If I cut off your rear, how will you ever get through? What a witless fool—to fall straight into my trap!” He immediately ordered his troops to prepare for battle: “Tonight, cook at the second watch as well. At the third watch, leave the city and lie in ambush where the trees and undergrowth are thick. Wait until Zhang Fei has passed through the narrow throat of the road; when the baggage train arrives, listen for the drums and charge out together.” The command was passed. As night approached, Yan Yan’s entire army ate its fill, armed itself completely, slipped quietly out of the city, and lay scattered in ambush, awaiting the drum signal. Yan Yan himself led a dozen or so subordinate generals, dismounted, and concealed himself in the woods. Sometime after the third watch, they saw in the distance Zhang Fei himself at the head, spear held crosswise and horse at a gallop, quietly leading his army forward. After they had gone no more than three or four li, the wagons, equipment, men, and horses began following from the rear in a steady stream. Yan Yan saw everything clearly and ordered the drums beaten; the ambushers rose on every side. Just as they rushed to seize the baggage train, a gong sounded behind them and a body of troops swept in, shouting, “Old thief, do not flee! We have been waiting for you!” Yan Yan wheeled around and saw at their head a great general with a panther’s head, round glaring eyes, a swallow’s jaw, and a tiger’s whiskers, wielding an eighteen-foot serpent spear and riding a dark black horse. It was Zhang Fei. Gongs thundered on every side as the troops charged in. At the sight of Zhang Fei, Yan Yan was at a loss what to do. They crossed horses, and before a single bout was over, Zhang Fei feigned an opening. Yan Yan slashed at him with his blade. Zhang Fei dodged, drove in close, seized Yan Yan by the gap in his armor, captured him alive, and hurled him to the ground. The soldiers rushed forward and bound him with ropes. It turned out that the Zhang Fei who had passed earlier was an impostor. Foreseeing that Yan Yan would use drums as his signal, Zhang Fei had chosen the sounding of gongs as his own. At the sound of the gongs, all his troops converged, and more than half the soldiers of Yi Province cast off their armor, reversed their weapons, and surrendered.

p.src: Zhang Fei fought his way to the walls of Ba Commandery, only to find that the troops behind him had already entered the city. Zhang Fei ordered that the common people not be harmed and issued proclamations to reassure them. The executioners brought Yan Yan forward. Zhang Fei sat in the hall, but Yan Yan refused to kneel. Glaring and grinding his teeth, Zhang Fei thundered, “When a great general came against you, why did you not surrender, but dared resist him?” Without the least sign of fear, Yan Yan shouted back, “You faithless men have invaded our province and commanderies! Here there are generals who will lose their heads, but none who will surrender!” Zhang Fei flew into a rage and ordered the men beside him to behead Yan Yan. Yan Yan shouted, “You thieving wretch! If you mean to behead me, then do it. Why all this anger?” Seeing Yan Yan’s mighty bearing and unchanging expression, Zhang Fei’s anger turned to delight. He descended the steps, ordered the guards away, personally untied Yan Yan, gave him a robe to wear, and helped him to the seat of honor in the center. Then he bowed his head and said, “My words just now were offensive; I beg you not to hold them against me. I have long known that you, veteran general, are a man of heroic mettle.” Moved by his kindness and sense of honor, Yan Yan surrendered. A later poet praised Yan Yan in these lines:
